## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Sammodamānajātaka* (Ja 33) is a single-stanza birth story from the Pali *Jātaka* collection [Fausböll 1877]. According to its commentary, the Buddha delivered the story while residing at the Banyan-grove (Nigrodhārāma) near Kapilavatthu, prompted by a dispute among his kinsmen concerning a porter's head-pad (*cumbatakalaha*), an incident also connected with the *Kuṇālajātaka* [Fausböll 1877].

In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta is reborn as a wise quail who leads a large flock [Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1877; Söhnen-Thieme]. When a fowler (*sākunika*) catches them in his net, the Bodhisatta instructs the birds to cooperate and lift the net together onto a thorn bush, allowing them to escape underneath [Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1877]. The fowler repeatedly returns home empty-handed; when his wife suspects his fidelity, he reassures her with the Jātaka's sole canonical verse (*gāthā*), predicting that the birds fly away together only while concord reigns (*sammodamānā gacchanti jālam ādāya pakkhino*), but will fall into his power once they quarrel [Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1877; Söhnen-Thieme]. Eventually, an argument over accidentally treading on another's head causes disunity; the birds refuse to cooperate, and the fowler captures them all [Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1877]. In the conclusion (*samodhāna*), the foolish, contentious quail is identified as Devadatta and the wise quail as the Bodhisatta, while the fowler remains unidentified [Fausböll 1877; Söhnen-Thieme].
